planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; velvet begonia is more sun- and drought-tolerant than most begonias and rots quickly in constantly wet soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; velvet begonia is more sun- and drought-tolerant than most begonias and rots quickly in constantly wet soil. Thick, rounded, succulent leaves are densely covered in soft, silvery-white, felted hairs that give the whole plant a plush, frosted appearance and a texture unlike almost any other begonia, with clusters of white, waxy, fragrant flowers appearing over a long season. Native to coastal sand dunes and rocky outcrops in Brazil and Uruguay, it is unusually tolerant of full sun, salt spray, and drought for a begonia, reflecting its exposed native habitat, and it thrives with more light and less water than the shade-loving rex and cane-type begonias more commonly grown. Water only when the soil has dried and provide bright light for the fullest, most compact growth and best flowering.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained, chunky potting mix; Rajah begonia wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained, chunky potting mix; Rajah begonia wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11. Compact, rounded, quilted leaves are patterned in deep bronze-green with a striking metallic silver overlay and contrasting reddish veins and undersides, forming a low, rhizomatous rosette rather than the tall canes of angel wing begonias. Native to the rainforests of Borneo, it belongs to a group of rhizomatous begonias prized among collectors for their compact scale and intricately patterned foliage, well suited to a terrarium, wardian case, or humid grow-tent setup rather than an average dry living room. Provide steady humidity above 60 percent where possible, keep soil evenly moist but never soggy, and avoid direct sun, which scorches its delicate leaves.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; shield-leaf begonia wants consistent humidity and moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; shield-leaf begonia wants consistent humidity and moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11. Rounded, olive-green leaves are attached to their stalks from the center of the leaf rather than the edge, a peltate arrangement that gives the foliage a distinctive umbrella-like symmetry, with small white to pale pink flowers rising above the foliage on slender stems. Native to Central American cloud forests, it forms a tidy, low, rhizomatous clump well suited to a terrarium or humid shaded windowsill, its neat, symmetrical leaf shape providing a calm textural contrast to the more heavily patterned rex-type begonias. Keep humidity high, water when the soil surface begins to dry, and avoid direct sun, which quickly scorches the leaves.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; sun-changing begonia colors most dramatically with bright indirect light and consistent humidity.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; sun-changing begonia colors most dramatically with bright indirect light and consistent humidity. This unusual Brazilian species is named for its remarkable ability to shift leaf color through the day, its rounded, lightly ruffled leaves turning from soft chartreuse-green to a striking golden yellow-green in bright light before settling back to green in lower light, an adaptive color response rather than fixed variegation. Its ever-changing foliage color makes it a conversation piece among collectors, and it is best displayed where its subtle daily transformation can actually be observed, such as a bright kitchen or sunroom window. Keep humidity moderate to high, water when the soil surface begins to dry, and protect from harsh direct sun, which can scorch rather than simply color the leaves.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Baker's anthurium is a compact epiphyte well suited to a hanging basket or mounted display.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Baker's anthurium is a compact epiphyte well suited to a hanging basket or mounted display. Long, narrow, leathery, strap-shaped leaves radiate outward from a short stem in a fountain-like rosette, quite different from the broad heart-shaped leaves of the florist's anthurium, and mature plants produce small greenish spathes followed by decorative clusters of bright orange-red berries that persist for months. Native to Central American cloud forests, where it grows as an epiphyte on tree branches, it appreciates the same loose, fast-draining, orchid-bark-based mix and bright, filtered light as other epiphytic anthuriums. Water when the mix approaches dryness, maintain high humidity, and avoid dense, water-retentive potting soil that encourages root rot.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Silvery Ann satin pothos holds its heavier silver variegation best with consistent bright indirect light.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Silvery Ann satin pothos holds its heavier silver variegation best with consistent bright indirect light. Thick, quilted, dark green leaves are heavily overlaid with large, irregular patches of metallic silver, carrying noticeably more silver coverage than the standard satin pothos, giving trailing stems a frostier, more dramatic shimmer. Native to Southeast Asian forests, it is a true climbing aroid in the wild but is most often grown trailing from a hanging basket or shelf indoors, where its thick, semi-succulent leaves tolerate drier conditions and lower humidity better than many other trailing aroids. Let the potting mix dry between waterings, provide bright indirect light to maximize the silver patterning, and mist occasionally to keep leaves dust-free and glossy.
